newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: UN-brokered W.Sahara talks seek to break deadlock.
newsitem.headline: UN-brokered W.Sahara talks seek to break deadlock.

text.p: Morocco and its Western Sahara opponents, the Polisario Front, start a rare round of direct talks in Lisbon on Monday under pressure from the United Nations to break a deadlock over the future of the mineral-rich former Spanish colony.

Former U.S. secretary of state James Baker, recently named special envoy by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, called the meeting after sensing signs of movement when he met all sides to the long-running dispute separately in London earlier this month.
A U.N.-brokered ceasefire has been in force in the vast desert territory since 1991 but attempts to convene a referendum on its future, initially set for January 1992, have repeatedly failed.

Morocco, which controls some four-fifths of the 250,000 square km (100,000 sq mile) territory, with its huge potassium mines and rich Atlantic fishing grounds, and the Algeria-backed Polisario cannot agree on who should be allowed to vote.

The Polisario, who fought a 15-year bushfire war against Morocco after the Spanish withdrew in 1976, wants the referendum limited to the 75,000 people registered as living in the Western Sahara before the conflict erupted.

Morocco, to whom Spain ceded administration of the territory jointly with Mauritania, wants to include the 120,000 people who have since moved into the Western Sahara, which has a significant nomad populaton.
Baker said in London that Morocco was now prepared to reduce its demands, while the Polisario had agreed to stop boycotting attempts to identify who was eligible to vote.
"This does not mean we will succeed. But at least it means we are back on track," he said in London about the Lisbon meeting.
Algeria and Mauritius will also send envoys to the three days of talks to be held in an old fort just outside Lisbon.

Annan has asked Baker, whose past diplomatic successes include getting Israel and the Palestinians together for the Madrid conference that was key to the Middle East peace process, to decide whether the Saharan stalemate can be broken under the existing plan or whether a new approach is going to be needed.

The U.N., which recently renewed the mandate of its Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) for another four months until September 30, has become increasingly frustrated at the costs of its effort to bring about a solution.
But it also fears the destabilising effect on the region of any resumption of the desert war in which an unknown number of people were killed.

Diplomatic sources said that they doubted the talks, which follow an unsuccessful meeting between Moroccan and Polisario representatives last year, would produce any dramatic breakthough. But they said that they might at least lay down an agenda for future negotiations.
